column9: Acceleration is –
column14: The rate of change of velocity
column15: The distance an object travels per unit of time
column16: The product of an object's mass and velocity
column17: How far an object is from its reference point
column28: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity: how fast the velocity changes over time. Distance per unit of time is speed, and mass × velocity is momentum.
column29: Acceleration is about change. Which choice talks about velocity changing?

column9: When the velocity of an object changes, the object is ___.
column28: When the velocity of an object changes, the object is accelerating. Any change in velocity (speed or direction) is acceleration.
column29: What is the name for the rate of change of velocity? Use its -ing form.

column9: In the acceleration formula, the small f in v_{f} stands for ___.
column28: v_{f} is the final velocity (where the object ends up) and v_{i} is the initial velocity (where it starts). Acceleration = (final − initial) / time.
column29: v_{i} is where the velocity starts; v_{f} is where it ___.

column9: A car going around a curve at a constant 35 mi/h is not accelerating, because its speed does not change.
column28: False. Velocity includes direction. Going around a curve changes the car's direction, so its velocity changes, and the car is accelerating even though the speed stays at 35 mi/h.
column29: Velocity is speed and direction. Is the direction staying the same on a curve?

column9: A car moving in a straight line at a constant 100 km/h has a positive acceleration, because it is moving forward fast.
column28: False. Speed is not changing and direction is not changing, so velocity is not changing. No change in velocity means zero acceleration, no matter how fast the car is going.
column29: Is the speed changing? Is the direction changing? Acceleration only happens when velocity changes.

column9: What is the SI unit of acceleration?
column28: Acceleration is measured in meters per second squared, m/s^{2}. m/s is the unit for speed and velocity, kg·m/s is momentum, and m is distance.
column29: Acceleration is a change in velocity (m/s) divided by time (s).

column9: Match each quantity to its unit.
column28: Distance is in m, time in s, speed and velocity in m/s, acceleration in m/s^{2}, and momentum in kg·m/s.
column29: Acceleration's unit has a second "per second" in it. Momentum's unit has mass in it.

column9: Liv's go-kart starts from rest and reaches 12 m/s in 4 s. What is its acceleration in m/s^{2}?
column28: Formula: a = (v_{f} − v_{i}) / t. Set Up: a = (12 m/s − 0 m/s) / 4 s. Answer: 3 m/s^{2}.
column29: "From rest" means v_{i} = 0 m/s. Subtract, then divide by the time.

column9: A car speeds up from 0 km/h to 36 km/h in 4 seconds. What is its acceleration in km/h/s?
column28: Formula: a = (v_{f} − v_{i}) / t. Set Up: a = (36 km/h − 0 km/h) / 4 s. Answer: 9 km/h/s (the car gains 9 km/h every second).
column29: Keep the speeds in km/h and the time in seconds; the unit becomes km/h/s.

column9: Which formula is used to calculate acceleration?
column28: Acceleration = (final velocity − initial velocity) / time, a = (v_{f} − v_{i}) / t. Subtracting in the other order flips the sign, and d/t is speed.
column29: Acceleration is the change in velocity divided by time. Change = final minus initial.

column9: Which is NOT an example of acceleration?
column14: A jet taking off down a runway
column15: A bus braking to stop at a red light
column16: A runner turning the corner on a track
column17: A car driving at a constant 60 mph on a straight highway
column28: A car at a constant 60 mph on a straight highway has no change in speed or direction, so its acceleration is zero. Taking off, braking, and turning all change velocity.
column29: Acceleration needs a change in speed or a change in direction. Which choice has neither?

column9: A horse trotting at 3 m/s speeds up to 15 m/s in 6 s. What is the horse's acceleration in m/s^{2}?
column28: Formula: a = (v_{f} − v_{i}) / t. Set Up: a = (15 m/s − 3 m/s) / 6 s = 12 m/s / 6 s. Answer: 2 m/s^{2}. Common mistake: dividing 15 by 6 without subtracting the starting velocity.
column29: Subtract the starting velocity from the final velocity first, then divide by the time.

column9: A jet's velocity goes from 0 m/s to 80 m/s as it moves forward down the runway. Its acceleration is –
column17: Impossible to tell without the jet's mass
column28: The jet is speeding up in the forward direction, so v_{f} − v_{i} is positive and the acceleration is positive. For an object moving forward (the positive direction), positive = speeding up and negative = slowing down.
column29: Is the final velocity bigger or smaller than the initial velocity? What sign does v_{f} − v_{i} have?

column9: Acceleration that makes a moving object slow down is called ___.
column28: Negative acceleration is called deceleration: the object is slowing down.
column29: It is the word for acceleration with a prefix that means "down" or "away."

column9: A toy rocket car starts from rest and accelerates at 2 m/s^{2} for 8 s, moving forward. What is its final velocity in m/s?
column28: Formula: v_{f} = v_{i} + a × t. Set Up: v_{f} = 0 m/s + (2 m/s^{2} × 8 s). Answer: 16 m/s forward.
column29: From rest, the car gains the same amount of velocity every second. Multiply acceleration by time.

column9: Bradley's bike is moving at 2.0 m/s. He pedals harder and reaches 16 m/s in 3.5 s. What is his acceleration in m/s^{2}?
column28: Formula: a = (v_{f} − v_{i}) / t. Set Up: a = (16 m/s − 2.0 m/s) / 3.5 s = 14 m/s / 3.5 s. Answer: 4 m/s^{2}.
column29: Find the change in velocity first (final − initial), then divide by the time.

column9: Jae is riding his scooter at 15 m/s. He hits a curb and slides to a stop in 3 s. What was his acceleration in m/s^{2}? Take forward as positive.
column28: Formula: a = (v_{f} − v_{i}) / t. Set Up: a = (0 m/s − 15 m/s) / 3 s. Answer: -5 m/s^{2}. The negative sign means he is slowing down (deceleration).
column29: "Slides to a stop" means the final velocity is 0 m/s. Final minus initial will be negative.

column9: A car moving forward at 24 m/s brakes with an acceleration of −3 m/s^{2} for 5 s. What is the car's velocity after the 5 s, in m/s?
column28: Formula: v_{f} = v_{i} + a × t. Set Up: v_{f} = 24 m/s + (−3 m/s^{2} × 5 s) = 24 m/s − 15 m/s. Answer: 9 m/s forward.
column29: Multiply the acceleration by the time to get the change in velocity. A negative change means you subtract.

column9: A motorcycle has an acceleration of 4 m/s^{2}. How much time does it need to reach a velocity of 26 m/s from rest? Answer in s.
column28: Formula: t = (v_{f} − v_{i}) / a. Set Up: t = (26 m/s − 0 m/s) / 4 m/s^{2}. Answer: 6.5 s.
column29: Rearrange a = (v_{f} − v_{i}) / t so time is by itself: divide the change in velocity by the acceleration.

column9: Andrea is skating forward at 5 m/s. She speeds up with an acceleration of 1.5 m/s^{2} for 6 s. What is her final velocity in m/s?
column28: Formula: v_{f} = v_{i} + a × t. Set Up: v_{f} = 5 m/s + (1.5 m/s^{2} × 6 s) = 5 m/s + 9 m/s. Answer: 14 m/s forward. Common mistake: forgetting to add the starting 5 m/s.
column29: Find how much velocity she gains (a × t), then add it to where she started.

column9: A delivery truck on Broadway slows from 25 m/s to 10 m/s in 5 s. What is its acceleration in m/s^{2}? Take forward as positive.
column28: Formula: a = (v_{f} − v_{i}) / t. Set Up: a = (10 m/s − 25 m/s) / 5 s = −15 m/s / 5 s. Answer: -3 m/s^{2}. The truck is slowing down, so the answer is negative.
column29: Final minus initial. The final velocity is smaller, so watch the sign.

column9: A car merging onto Highway 29 speeds up from 20 km/h to 65 km/h in 5 seconds. What is its acceleration in km/h/s?
column28: Formula: a = (v_{f} − v_{i}) / t. Set Up: a = (65 km/h − 20 km/h) / 5 s = 45 km/h / 5 s. Answer: 9 km/h/s.
column29: The speeds are in km/h and the time is in seconds, so the answer unit is km/h/s. Subtract first.

column9: A cyclist moving at 8 m/s accelerates at 3 m/s^{2}. How many seconds does it take her to reach 20 m/s? Answer in s.
column28: Formula: t = (v_{f} − v_{i}) / a. Set Up: t = (20 m/s − 8 m/s) / 3 m/s^{2} = 12 m/s / 3 m/s^{2}. Answer: 4 s.
column29: Find the change in velocity, then divide by the acceleration.

column9: Why is the unit for acceleration m/s^{2}?
column14: Meters are multiplied by seconds two times
column15: A velocity in m/s is divided by a time in s
column16: Distance in m is divided by time in s
column17: A velocity in m/s is multiplied by a time in s
column28: Acceleration = change in velocity / time, so the unit is (m/s) / s = m/s/s, written m/s^{2}. It means meters per second, every second.
column29: Write the units into the formula: velocity unit on top, time unit on the bottom.

column9: To calculate an object's acceleration, which three values do you need?
column16: Initial velocity, final velocity, and time
column28: a = (v_{f} − v_{i}) / t uses initial velocity, final velocity, and time. Distance, mass, and average speed are not used to calculate acceleration.
column29: Look at the acceleration formula. Which letters appear in it?

column9: Raegan rides a merry-go-round at a constant speed of 3 m/s. Is she accelerating?
column14: No, because her speed is not changing
column15: No, because she ends up back where she started
column16: Yes, because her speed keeps increasing
column17: Yes, because her direction keeps changing
column28: Yes. Her speed is constant, but she is moving in a circle, so her direction keeps changing. A change in direction is a change in velocity, which is acceleration.
column29: Velocity is speed and direction. Which one is changing on a merry-go-round?

column9: A sled has an acceleration of 3 m/s^{2} down a hill. This means –
column14: Its velocity increases by 3 m/s every second
column16: Its speed stays at 3 m/s the whole way
column17: It takes 3 seconds to reach the bottom
column28: 3 m/s^{2} = 3 (m/s)/s: the sled's velocity goes up by 3 m/s every second. It does not mean it travels 3 m each second or has a top speed of 3 m/s.
column29: Read the unit as (m/s) per second. What changes by 3 every second?

column9: An object moving at a high speed must have a large acceleration.
column28: False. Acceleration depends on how fast velocity changes, not on how fast the object is going. A jet cruising in a straight line at a constant 250 m/s has zero acceleration.
column29: Think of something going very fast in a straight line at a steady speed. Is its velocity changing?

column9: Put the steps for solving an acceleration problem in order.
column15: Write the answer with units, like m/s^{2}
column16: Write the formula a = (v_{f} − v_{i}) / t
column17: Divide the change in velocity by the time
column18: Set up: plug in the numbers with their units
column28: Formula / Set Up / Answer: write the formula, plug in the numbers with units, subtract v_{f} − v_{i}, divide by time, then write the answer with units (m/s^{2}).
column29: Mr. Erickson's format is Formula, Set Up, Answer with units. Subtraction in the top happens before dividing.

column9: A train slows from 90 km/h to 30 km/h in 12 seconds as it pulls into Cadott. What is its acceleration in km/h/s? Take forward as positive.
column28: Formula: a = (v_{f} − v_{i}) / t. Set Up: a = (30 km/h − 90 km/h) / 12 s = −60 km/h / 12 s. Answer: -5 km/h/s (it is slowing down).
column29: Final minus initial, then divide by the time in seconds. Slowing down gives a negative answer.

column9: A sprinter leaving the blocks is moving forward at 2 m/s and accelerates at 0.8 m/s^{2} for 5 s. What is her velocity after 5 s, in m/s?
column28: Formula: v_{f} = v_{i} + a × t. Set Up: v_{f} = 2 m/s + (0.8 m/s^{2} × 5 s) = 2 m/s + 4 m/s. Answer: 6 m/s forward.
column29: Multiply acceleration by time to find the velocity gained, then add the starting velocity.

column9: Which of these could be units of acceleration? Select all that apply.
column28: An acceleration unit is a velocity unit divided by a time unit: m/s^{2}, km/h/s, and mi/h/s all fit. m/s and km/h are speed units, and kg·m/s is momentum.
column29: Look for a speed unit followed by "per second" (or a squared second).

column9: A car moving at 30 m/s brakes with an acceleration of −5 m/s^{2}. How many seconds does it take to come to a stop? Answer in s.
column28: Formula: t = (v_{f} − v_{i}) / a. Set Up: t = (0 m/s − 30 m/s) / −5 m/s^{2} = −30 m/s / −5 m/s^{2}. Answer: 6 s (a negative divided by a negative is positive).
column29: Come to a stop means v_{f} = 0. Divide the change in velocity by the acceleration and watch the signs.

column9: Marcus is driving forward at 18 m/s and slows down with an acceleration of −2.5 m/s^{2} for 4 s. What is his velocity after 4 s, in m/s?
column28: Formula: v_{f} = v_{i} + a × t. Set Up: v_{f} = 18 m/s + (−2.5 m/s^{2} × 4 s) = 18 m/s − 10 m/s. Answer: 8 m/s forward.
column29: a × t tells how much velocity changes. With a negative acceleration, that change is subtracted.

column9: Riley calculates a = (4 m/s − 16 m/s) / 3 s = −4 m/s^{2} for a bike moving forward. What does the negative sign tell you?
column28: For an object moving in the positive (forward) direction, a negative acceleration means it is slowing down (deceleration). It is still moving forward, just losing speed.
column29: Compare the final and initial velocities. Did the bike get faster or slower?

column9: A sports car goes from 0 to 60 mph in 4.2 s. (Watch units: 60 mph = 26.8 m/s.) What is its acceleration in m/s^{2}?
column28: Convert first: 60 mph = 26.8 m/s. Formula: a = (v_{f} − v_{i}) / t. Set Up: a = (26.8 m/s − 0 m/s) / 4.2 s. Answer: 6.381 m/s^{2} (about 6.38). Common mistake: using 60 instead of 26.8.
column29: The answer is in m/s^{2}, so change mph to m/s with the given fact before you use the formula.

column9: Maya is driving at 30 mph when a deer runs out, and she brakes to a stop in 2.5 s. (Watch units: 30 mph = 13.4 m/s.) What is her acceleration in m/s^{2}? Take forward as positive.
column28: Convert: 30 mph = 13.4 m/s. Formula: a = (v_{f} − v_{i}) / t. Set Up: a = (0 m/s − 13.4 m/s) / 2.5 s. Answer: -5.36 m/s^{2}. Negative because she is slowing down.
column29: Change mph to m/s first. Brakes to a stop means v_{f} = 0, so the answer will be negative.

column9: A car on Highway 29 accelerates from rest to 72 km/h in 8 s. (Watch units: 72 km/h = 20 m/s.) What is its acceleration in m/s^{2}?
column28: Convert: 72 km/h = 20 m/s. Formula: a = (v_{f} − v_{i}) / t. Set Up: a = (20 m/s − 0 m/s) / 8 s. Answer: 2.5 m/s^{2}. Using 72 would give 9 km/h/s, which is the wrong unit.
column29: The answer must be in m/s^{2}, so put the velocity in m/s before dividing by seconds.

column9: A freight train starts from rest and reaches 30 m/s in 1.5 minutes. (Watch units: 1 minute = 60 s.) What is its acceleration in m/s^{2}?
column28: Convert: 1.5 min × 60 s/min = 90 s. Formula: a = (v_{f} − v_{i}) / t. Set Up: a = (30 m/s − 0 m/s) / 90 s. Answer: 0.333 m/s^{2} (about 0.33). Common mistake: dividing by 1.5 and getting 20.
column29: Change the time to seconds first, then use the formula.

column9: After accelerating forward at 2 m/s^{2} for 7 s, a car is moving at 30 m/s. How fast was it moving at the start, in m/s?
column28: Formula: v_{f} = v_{i} + a × t, so v_{i} = v_{f} − a × t. Set Up: v_{i} = 30 m/s − (2 m/s^{2} × 7 s) = 30 m/s − 14 m/s. Answer: 16 m/s. Check: 16 + 14 = 30.
column29: The car gained a × t of velocity during the 7 s. Take that gain away from the final velocity.

column9: A school bus moving at 25 m/s brakes with an acceleration of −3.2 m/s^{2} until it is moving at 9 m/s. How many seconds does this take? Answer in s.
column28: Formula: t = (v_{f} − v_{i}) / a. Set Up: t = (9 m/s − 25 m/s) / −3.2 m/s^{2} = −16 m/s / −3.2 m/s^{2}. Answer: 5 s.
column29: Find the change in velocity (final − initial), then divide by the acceleration. Two negatives make a positive.

column9: A motorcycle accelerates at 12 km/h/s. How many seconds does it take to go from 30 km/h to 102 km/h? Answer in s.
column28: Formula: t = (v_{f} − v_{i}) / a. Set Up: t = (102 km/h − 30 km/h) / 12 km/h/s = 72 km/h / 12 km/h/s. Answer: 6 s. The km/h cancel, leaving seconds.
column29: Divide the change in speed (km/h) by the acceleration (km/h/s); km/h cancels and seconds are left.

column9: Which car has the greatest acceleration? Car A: 0 to 24 m/s in 6 s. Car B: 0 to 90 km/h in 5 s (90 km/h = 25 m/s). Car C: 10 m/s to 28 m/s in 4 s. Car D: 0 to 30 m/s in 8 s.
column28: Calculate each in m/s^{2}: A = 24/6 = 4; B = 25/5 = 5; C = (28 − 10)/4 = 4.5; D = 30/8 = 3.75. Car B is greatest. Car D reaches the highest speed but takes longer.
column29: Put every car in m/s first, then find (v_{f} − v_{i}) / t for each. Do not just pick the highest final speed.

column9: A skater moving forward slows from 12 m/s to 4 m/s in 4 s. Take forward as positive. Bradley writes a = (12 m/s − 4 m/s) / 4 s = 2 m/s^{2}. What is wrong?
column14: He should have multiplied by the time instead of dividing
column15: He should have added the velocities instead of subtracting
column16: He subtracted in the wrong order; the answer is −2 m/s^{2}
column17: Nothing; the answer is positive because the skater is still moving forward
column28: He subtracted in the wrong order. Correct Set Up: a = (4 m/s − 12 m/s) / 4 s = -2 m/s^{2}. The skater is slowing down, so the acceleration must be negative.
column29: The formula is final minus initial. Which velocity did Bradley put first?

column9: Liv says a car cruising in a straight line at a constant 100 km/h has a greater acceleration than a bike speeding up from 2 m/s to 6 m/s. Which response is correct?
column14: Liv is wrong; the car's acceleration is zero and the bike's is greater
column15: Liv is right, because 100 km/h is much faster than 6 m/s
column16: Liv is right, because the car covers more distance each second
column17: They have the same acceleration, because both are moving forward
column28: Liv is wrong. The car's velocity is not changing, so its acceleration is 0. The bike's velocity is changing, so it has an acceleration greater than 0. Acceleration measures change in velocity, not speed.
column29: Acceleration is about change. Which one is changing its velocity?

column9: A car moving forward at 40 km/h accelerates at 8 km/h/s for 4.5 seconds. What is its final velocity in km/h?
column28: Formula: v_{f} = v_{i} + a × t. Set Up: v_{f} = 40 km/h + (8 km/h/s × 4.5 s) = 40 km/h + 36 km/h. Answer: 76 km/h forward. The seconds cancel, leaving km/h.
column29: Multiply km/h/s by seconds to get km/h gained, then add it to the starting velocity.

column9: A plane lands moving at 70 m/s and comes to a stop on the runway in 0.4 minutes. (Watch units: 1 minute = 60 s.) What is its acceleration in m/s^{2}? Take forward as positive.
column28: Convert: 0.4 min × 60 s/min = 24 s. Formula: a = (v_{f} − v_{i}) / t. Set Up: a = (0 m/s − 70 m/s) / 24 s. Answer: -2.917 m/s^{2} (about −2.92). Dividing by 0.4 instead of 24 gives −175, which is far too big.
column29: Change minutes to seconds first. Coming to a stop means v_{f} = 0, so the answer is negative.

column9: A car accelerates from rest at 3.0 m/s^{2}. How many seconds does it take to reach 45 mph? (Watch units: 45 mph = 20.1 m/s.) Answer in s.
column28: Convert: 45 mph = 20.1 m/s. Formula: t = (v_{f} − v_{i}) / a. Set Up: t = (20.1 m/s − 0 m/s) / 3.0 m/s^{2}. Answer: 6.7 s. Using 45 would give 15 s, which is wrong because mph and m/s^{2} do not match.
column29: The acceleration is in m/s^{2}, so change mph to m/s before dividing.

column9: Each object moves forward in a straight line. Match each change in velocity to its acceleration.
column14: 0 m/s to 20 m/s in 4 s :: 5 m/s²
column15: 20 m/s to 0 m/s in 4 s :: −5 m/s²
column16: 4 m/s to 20 m/s in 8 s :: 2 m/s²
column17: 20 m/s to 4 m/s in 4 s :: −4 m/s²
column18: Stays at 20 m/s for 4 s :: 0 m/s²
column28: a = (v_{f} − v_{i}) / t for each: (20 − 0)/4 = 5; (0 − 20)/4 = -5; (20 − 4)/8 = 2; (4 − 20)/4 = -4; (20 − 20)/4 = 0 m/s^{2}. Slowing down gives a negative answer; no change gives zero.
column29: Do final minus initial for each one, then divide by the time. Keep the sign.

column9: A car is moving forward at 54 km/h when the driver brakes with an acceleration of −2.4 m/s^{2} for 5 s. (Watch units: 54 km/h = 15 m/s.) What is the car's velocity after 5 s, in m/s?
column28: Convert: 54 km/h = 15 m/s. Formula: v_{f} = v_{i} + a × t. Set Up: v_{f} = 15 m/s + (−2.4 m/s^{2} × 5 s) = 15 m/s − 12 m/s. Answer: 3 m/s forward.
column29: The acceleration is in m/s^{2}, so change the starting velocity to m/s first. Then find a × t and subtract it.
